events.label: Mexico City rises on the ruins
events.description: On the rubble of Tenochtitlan's great temple the Spanish raised the vast Metropolitan Cathedral and a grid of a capital — the new colonial city built literally on top of the one it destroyed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The conquest was made literal in stone: the Spanish demolished the Templo Mayor, the Aztecs' great twin-shrined pyramid, and used its very blocks to build their cathedral on the same spot. The new city was a deliberate erasure laid over the old one — but the old one keeps surfacing. The whole capital sits on the soft, drained lakebed of Tenochtitlan, so it has been sinking for centuries (parts of the historic center have dropped some 30 feet, and the cathedral visibly tilts). And the buried city refuses to stay buried: in 1978 electrical workers digging behind the cathedral struck a carved stone disc and uncovered the foundations of the Templo Mayor itself, which now sits excavated in the heart of the modern city — the destroyed Aztec capital clawing its way back into daylight beside the one built to replace it.

events.label: The Council of the Indies
events.description: Spain governed its sprawling new empire through the Council of the Indies, a body in Castile that wrote the laws, named the viceroys, and tried to rule two continents by letters that took months to cross the sea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Spain tried to govern half a world by mail. From a council chamber in Castile, a body of officials who had mostly never crossed the Atlantic wrote the laws for the Americas, appointed and recalled the viceroys, heard legal appeals, and tried to micromanage two continents — all by dispatches that took months each way and a year or more for a round trip. The lag built a famous loophole into colonial life, captured in the phrase "obedezco pero no cumplo" — "I obey but I do not comply" — by which a far-off official could formally bow to a royal order he had no intention of carrying out, knowing it would take ages for the crown to even notice. It is the bureaucratic root of the whole age's central tension: a king who claimed absolute power over a New World he could only reach by a letter that took half a year to arrive.

events.label: Spanish missions and reductions
events.description: Friars gathered scattered indigenous people into mission towns and reductions — part church, part labor camp, part refuge — the frontier institution that spread both Catholicism and colonial control.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The mission was a contradiction with walls. Friars gathered scattered indigenous people into planned towns (in Spanish, reducciones — literally "reductions," because the population was "reduced," gathered, into one place) where they were taught Christianity and European trades, protected to a degree from the worst of the slavers and labor-drafts — and also controlled, regimented, and exposed to the very diseases that crowding spread. The most striking experiment came later in Paraguay, where Jesuits built a network of self-governing Guaraní mission-towns so prosperous and autonomous they functioned almost as an independent state, until Spain and Portugal crushed them. The reduction is the conquest's softer face and its iron hand at once: shelter and cage, school and labor camp, the gentlest and most total instrument of colonial control on the same ground.

events.label: The Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan
events.description: Japan crucified twenty-six Christians at Nagasaki as the shogunate turned against the foreign faith — the first bloody sign that the Jesuit 'Christian century' would end in suppression and expulsion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The twenty-six included foreign missionaries and Japanese converts — among them three boys, the youngest about twelve. They were marched hundreds of miles in winter to Nagasaki and crucified together on a hill in 1597 as a public warning. It worked as one: Japan went on to ban Christianity outright and, over the following decades, hunted down believers with chilling ingenuity — most infamously the fumi-e, bronze plaques bearing Christian images that suspects were ordered to step on to prove they were not of the faith. Yet the religion didn't fully die. When Japan reopened to the world over two centuries later, missionaries were astonished to find communities of "hidden Christians" who had secretly kept a garbled, half-remembered version of the faith alive in total isolation for some 250 years.

events.label: Bernal Díaz writes the conquest
events.description: An old foot-soldier, Bernal Díaz del Castillo, wrote The True History of the Conquest of New Spain — a grumbling, vivid eyewitness account meant to put the common conquistador back in a story the captains had stolen.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He wrote out of indignation. Decades after the conquest, an old and half-blind Bernal Díaz read the polished official histories — especially the one by Cortés's own chaplain — that made the conquest a tale of one great captain's genius, and it galled him: he and the other common soldiers, and the tens of thousands of indigenous allies, had been written out of their own war. So he set down his True History to put them back in, apologizing for his plain soldier's style while delivering something the courtly chroniclers never could — the texture of it, the names of comrades and horses, the fear, the food, the small concrete things only a man who was there would remember. The result is one of the most vivid eyewitness accounts in all of history, and a reminder that even the conquerors fought over who got to own the story.

events.label: Sahagún's Florentine Codex
events.description: The Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún and his Nahua students compiled the Florentine Codex, a bilingual encyclopedia of Aztec life — much of what we know of the vanished world was recorded by the people who helped erase it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It is one of history's great acts of salvage by the destroyers. The friar Sahagún spent decades with Nahua elders and his own former students compiling a 12-book, roughly 2,400-page encyclopedia of Mexica life — religion, medicine, history, language, the natural world — written in parallel columns of Nahuatl and Spanish and illustrated with some 2,000 images drawn by indigenous artists. The irony is sharp: he built this monument to a civilization precisely to help his fellow missionaries recognize and stamp out its religion. So much of what we know about the Aztec world — including the Nahua side of the conquest itself, told by the people who survived it — comes down to us through a book made by a man trying to erase it. The surviving manuscript ended up in Florence, which is why we call it the Florentine Codex, and UNESCO has placed it on its Memory of the World register.

events.label: Camões sings the empire in verse
events.description: Luís de Camões published Os Lusíadas, the epic of da Gama's voyage that made Portugal's ocean exploits into national myth — a sailor-poet turning a trade route into Homeric legend.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Camões didn't just write about the age of voyages — he lived its dangers. He lost his right eye soldiering in North Africa, was jailed, and spent years knocking around Portugal's eastern empire, and the poem's survival is the stuff of legend: shipwrecked in the Mekong delta on his way home, he is said to have swum to shore with one arm while holding the only manuscript of his unfinished epic above the water with the other. Published in 1572, Os Lusíadas turned da Gama's trade voyage into a Homeric national myth, complete with Greek gods arguing over the Portuguese in the heavens. It became the founding text of Portuguese literature — the language is sometimes called "the language of Camões" — and the proof that the age of exploration was busy mythologizing itself almost before it was over.

events.label: Cieza de León chronicles the Andes
events.description: The young soldier Pedro Cieza de León wrote a careful, humane chronicle of Peru and the Inca world he marched through — among the first Europeans to treat a conquered civilization as worth understanding.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He is sometimes called the "prince of chroniclers," and what makes him remarkable is the method behind it: as he marched through Peru as a teenage soldier, he kept notes — by his own account writing them up at night after the day's exhausting travel, while his comrades rested — questioning Inca elders and recording the roads, the ruins, the customs, and the recent horrors of the conquest with a curiosity and fairness rare for his time. He treated the conquered Andean world as a real civilization worth understanding rather than scenery to be plundered, and his chronicle is one of the best windows we have onto the Inca state just as it was being destroyed. The deep irony of this whole chapter sits in men like him: the people who recorded the vanishing world were often the very soldiers who helped make it vanish.

events.label: The galleon, ship of the silver age
events.description: Bigger and more heavily gunned than the carrack, the galleon became the workhorse of the Atlantic treasure fleets and the Pacific run — the armed cargo ship that carried the world's silver and fought off its pirates.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The galleon was the answer to a single problem: how do you build a ship that is both a fat cargo hauler and a warship able to fight off the navies and pirates who want what's inside it? The design trimmed the old carrack's towering, top-heavy castles, sat lower and longer in the water, and lined the hull with gun decks — a vessel that could cross an ocean stuffed with silver and still throw a broadside. The Manila galleons that ran the Pacific were the giants of the type, some of the largest wooden ships of their day, built in the Philippines from dense tropical hardwoods that resisted the cannon and the sea better than European oak. For two and a half centuries the galleon was the literal vehicle of the world's wealth, the ship that carried globalization across two oceans.

events.label: The treasure fleets sail in convoy
events.description: Spain organized its American silver into the flota system — great escorted convoys that crossed the Atlantic together for safety, the financial bloodstream of an empire and the prize every privateer dreamed of taking.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The logic of the convoy was strength in numbers: rather than send lone treasure ships to be picked off by pirates, Spain gathered the year's silver into great escorted fleets that crossed the Atlantic together on a fixed schedule, gathering at Caribbean ports before the dash to Seville. For most of two centuries it worked astonishingly well — the system was robbed wholesale only a handful of times. The most spectacular was in 1628, when the Dutch privateer Piet Heyn captured an entire Spanish silver fleet off Cuba without losing a man, a haul so vast it funded the Dutch war against Spain and made him a national hero (Dutch children still sing a song about it). When the fleet didn't come — sunk by a hurricane, or held in port — a king on the other side of the ocean couldn't pay his armies.

events.label: The Northwest Passage obsession
events.description: Convinced of a frozen shortcut to Asia over the top of America, English captains threw lives and fortunes at the Northwest Passage for centuries — the great geographic fantasy the age refused to give up.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The dream made a kind of desperate sense: Spain and Portugal controlled the southern routes around Africa and South America, so England and its rivals convinced themselves there had to be a way through over the top of North America. There wasn't — not a usable one. For more than three centuries explorers hurled themselves at the frozen maze of the Arctic and died for it, most catastrophically Sir John Franklin's expedition in the 1840s, whose entire crew of 129 vanished into the ice (recent searches finally found their lost ships only in the 2010s). The passage was not actually navigated end to end until 1906, by Roald Amundsen — and was so choked with ice as to be commercially useless. The bitter irony of the age's last great geographic fantasy: the shortcut was real, but it took 400 years and a warming climate to make it anything but a death trap.

events.label: The Plymouth Pilgrims
events.description: Religious separatists crossed on the Mayflower and founded Plymouth Colony in New England — the strain of northern settlement driven less by gold than by the search for a place to worship freely.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: They were aiming somewhere else entirely. The Pilgrims had a patent to settle near the mouth of the Hudson, in the northern reaches of Virginia, but storms and bad navigation dumped the Mayflower far to the north on Cape Cod — outside any government's authority, which is why, before going ashore, the men signed the Mayflower Compact, an agreement to rule themselves by majority consent that later generations would mythologize as a seed of American democracy. Their survival hinged on a stroke of dark luck: the spot they chose had been a thriving Wampanoag village until an epidemic, carried by earlier European contact, had killed most of its people just a few years before, leaving cleared fields and stored seed for the newcomers to use. Even the colony built on faith rather than gold was, in the end, planted in ground emptied by the same Old World diseases that hollowed out two continents.
